extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy/economic history
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how cities and towns arose and how commerce and municipal institutions contributed to agricultural improvement, manufacture, and political power after the fall of the Roman Empire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes that estimate profits by stock (taille) discourage improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The taille is a tax upon the supposed profits of the farmer, which they estimate by the stock that he has upon the farm. It is his interest, therefore, to appear to have as little as possible, and consequently to employ as little as possible in its cultivation, and none in its improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such taxes hinder accumulated stock from being employed on land and may act as an effective prohibition of improvement; they may also carry social stigma that deters tenants from acquiring stock. Examples/analogues: the taille in France; ancient tenths and fifteenths in England.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure and rent structure determine incentives to improve land (farmer vs proprietor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The farmer, compared with the proprietor, is as a merchant who trades with borrowed money, compared with one who trades with his own. The lands cultivated by the farmer must... be improved more slowly than those cultivated by the proprietor, on account of the large share of the produce which is consumed in the rent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High rents and lack of proprietorship mean that farmers cannot reinvest produce into improvement. Proprietors are more likely to apply capital to increase land value; tenant farmers face disincentives because returns are captured by rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social status of cultivators affects capital allocation to agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: The yeomanry are regarded as an inferior rank of people... It can seldom happen... that a man of any considerable stock should quit the superior, in order to place himself in an inferior station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When farming is socially low-status, people with accumulated capital avoid entering it, reducing capital flow into agricultural improvement; reflects cultural/institutional barriers to occupational mobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of exportation and restraints on inland commerce impede cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancient policy... was unfavourable to the improvement and cultivation of land, first, by the general prohibition of the exportation of corn... and, secondly, by the restraints which were laid upon the inland commerce... by the absurd laws against engrossers, regraters, and forestallers, and by the privileges of fairs and markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade restrictions both on export and internal commerce reduce market access and prices for producers, thereby discouraging investment in cultivation. Historical examples include export prohibitions in ancient Italy and medieval laws against certain traders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal legal privileges create freedom and economic agency for burghers
rubrics_metrics.description: Privileges... that they might give away their own daughters in marriage without the consent of their lord, that upon their death their own children... should succeed to their goods, and that they might dispose of their own effects by will... the principal attributes of villanage and slavery being thus taken away from them, they now at least became really free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting personal property and familial autonomy converted town inhabitants from near-servile condition to free burghers, enabling accumulation of capital and independent economic activity. These legal changes often accompanied grants of farm-rent and civic corporations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal self-government and permanent fiscal arrangements foster security
rubrics_metrics.description: They were generally at the same time erected into a commonalty or corporation, with the privilege of having magistrates and a town-council of their own, of making bye-laws for their own government, of building walls for their own defence... the farm of the town was... granted... in fee, that is for ever, reserving a rent certain, never afterwards to be augmented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perpetual farm-rents and corporate municipal institutions reduced arbitrary exactions, provided local governance, and created security necessary for commerce and industry. Examples: free burghs, exemption from county courts, local judicial jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political alliances (king and burghers) shape granting of urban privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual interest... disposed them to support the king, and the king to support them against the lords. They were the enemies of his enemies, and it was his interest to render them as secure and independent of those enemies as he could.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereigns granted towns privileges as a strategic counterweight to barons; princes in bad standing with barons were more liberal in grants (examples: King John, Philip I/King Lewis). Political context explains when and why urban liberties expanded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cities act as sanctuaries for accumulated capital and entrepreneurial migrants
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever stock, therefore, accumulated in the hands of the industrious part of the inhabitants of the country, naturally took refuge in cities, as the only sanctuaries in which it could be secure... if he could conceal himself there from the pursuit of his lord for a year, he was free for ever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and physical protections in towns encouraged rural people to relocate with their savings, concentrating capital in urban centers and fostering industry and manufacture. This mechanism channels rural surplus into urban economic development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic position (ports/rivers) expands a city's market reach and wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The inhabitants of a city, situated near either the sea-coast or the banks of a navigable river... have a much wider range, and may draw them from the most remote corners of the world... A city might... grow up to great wealth and splendour, while not only the country in its neighbourhood... were in poverty and wretchedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access to maritime or riverine transport allows cities to trade at long distances, import luxuries, export manufactures, and grow wealthy independent of local agrarian prosperity. Examples: Venice, Genoa, Pisa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two paths for the origin of manufactures for distant sale
rubrics_metrics.description: Those manufactures... introduced... sometimes... by the violent operation... of particular merchants... (offspring of foreign commerce). At other times, manufactures... grow up naturally... by the gradual refinement of those household and coarser manufactures... (offspring of agriculture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign-commerce-born manufactures often use imported materials and are established by entrepreneurial projects (examples: Lucca silk to Venice, Spitalfields). Agriculture-born manufactures use domestic materials and emerge from local surpluses (examples: Leeds, Halifax, Sheffield). The origin affects materials, scale, and relation to agriculture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce improves the country via three channels
rubrics_metrics.description: The increase and riches of commercial and manufacturing towns contributed to the improvement and cultivation of the countries to which they belonged, in three different ways: First, by affording a great and ready market for the rude produce... Secondly, the wealth acquired by the inhabitants of cities was frequently employed in purchasing such lands as were to be sold... Thirdly... commerce and manufactures gradually introduced order and good government, and with them the liberty and security of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith highlights (1) market access raising prices and incentives for cultivation, (2) merchant capital purchase and improvement of land, and (3) institutional change (rule of law, security) as channels, noting the third as most important. Each channel has historical examples and mechanisms described in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for refined goods spurs domestic manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: The inhabitants of trading cities, by importing the improved manufactures and expensive luxuries of richer countries, afforded some food to the vanity of the great proprietors... A taste for the finer and more improved manufactures was, in this manner, introduced by foreign commerce into countries where no such works were carried on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imported luxuries create local demand that entrepreneurs meet by establishing domestic manufacture, reducing carriage costs and eventually producing for distant sale. Example: wool for English cloth exchanged for French wines and Flemish cloths; local manufacture later arises to meet demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce transforms feudal social structure by reallocating surplus
rubrics_metrics.description: In a country which has neither foreign commerce nor any of the finer manufactures, a great proprietor... consumes the whole [surplus] in rustic hospitality... He is at all times, therefore, surrounded with a multitude of retainers and dependants... Before the extension of commerce and manufactures... the hospitality of the rich and the great... exceeded every thing which... we can easily form a notion of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where markets for surplus do not exist, surplus sustains retainers and feudal dependency; commerce creates market outlets so surplus can be sold, reducing reliance on retainers and altering social/political relations (less patronage, fewer dependents). Historical anecdotes illustrate extreme hospitality and its decline with commerce.
